newsitem.title: UK: Bright outlook for UK-Latam air cargo trading.
newsitem.headline: Bright outlook for UK-Latam air cargo trading.

text.p: UK-Latin America air cargo business has generally prospered over recent weeks despite the strong value of sterling against local currencies, a Reuters survey shows.

And the outlook for the next few months looks good for UK airfreight exporters, forwarders and carriers involved in most Latam markets, especially as the pound had weakened by the end of its first week under a Labour government, observers noted.

While growth to the continent's major destination, Brazil, has of late been "slightly stunted", ex-Britain airfreight trading with Peru and Argentina in particular, and to a lesser extent to Mexico, Bolivia and Paraguay, continues on an upward trend, they added.
"There is no doubt that air cargo business to Brazil has fallen off slightly over the past month or so ," said Paul Ryan, Varig's UK cargo manager.
He added that British Airways, despite increasing its official London-Brazil cargo rates by 10 percent from April 1, was nevertheless "offering attractive prices" on the route.

"They (BA) are spot-rating regularly and, as the market has slowed down, strong competition from other major carriers like Air France, KLM and Lufthansa -- not to mention Iberia and TAP -- has also put downward pressure on rates," he said.
This is illustrated in Reuters' latest UK-Americas rates chart, which show the average London-Sao Paulo per kg/100 kg rate down three pence from last month to 1.77 stg.

Raeford Aviation Services sells 60 Latin American and Caribbean destinations in the UK through several cargo sales agency tie-ups with airlines including Cargopar, which flies from Miami to Paraguay and Brazil.
"Three to four years ago, there was tremendous demand for UK-Brazil airfreight capacity because at the time the economy of this very big market was on a high," said director Dennis Prince.
"Lately, I would describe the state of business on the route as just steady," he added.
Raeford is also cargo GSA in Britain for Lloyd Aero Boliviano (which serves Bolivia), Amerijet (Venezuela, Mexico and the Caribbean), Faucett (Peru), Lamsa (Guatemala) and Laker Airways (Miami).
Prince offered the following snapshot appraisals of ex-UK Latam airfreight markets:
Mexico: "Business is constantly up and down, with cargo mainly comprising electrical goods and machinery."
Bolivia: "A much steadier market, attracting a lot of general freight plus electrical goods and machinery parts.
Paraguay: "Fairly steady but only a very small market for the UK."
Peru: "Up and down, with strong demand one week and very little the next."
Kevin Durnin, managing director of Viking Freight Services, said that of the Latam markets he serves ex-UK, Peru had shown the strongest growth over recent weeks.

"President Fujimori appears to have stabilised the political and economic outlook of the country since the (April 22) hostage rescue (that ended a rebel siege of the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima)," said Durnin.

"The renewed business confidence has stimulated air cargo traffic from Britain. We are flying in everything and anything -- including two recent seven-tonne shipments of bouncy castles in one day," he said.
These were respectively flown on Leisure International Airways' Boeing 767-300ER flights from Manchester and London Gatwick to Miami, and on to Peru by Tower Air.
Durnin said that BA was continuing to offer very attractive pallet rate deals on its direct routes to Latin America, which he said he could not match with his transhipment services via Miami.
From Miami, Viking uses 14 carriers for onward southbound flights, including the previously mentioned Tower, plus Panama's COPA, El Salvador's TACA, Arrow Air, Fine Airlines and Challenge Air Cargo.

A new UK-Mexico competitor will appear in the form of Mexican all-cargo carrier MAS Air from May 17, when it will start weekly London Stansted-Mexico City-Guadalajara flights with a 38-tonne capacity hushkitted Boeing 707-320C.

"Although only seven of these services are scheduled up until the end of June, I am confident the series will continue at least until November," said Steve Dawkins, director of MAS Air's UK cargo GSA, Air Logistics.
"We are already getting bookings from pharmaceutical companies for large movements, including chemicals. We will also be carrying shipments of electrical goods and milk drinks," he said.
On return flights, mainly Mexican produced fruit will be flown, said Dawkins.

He described the state of the UK-Latin America air cargo market in general as "very buoyant" at present, adding that he had seen no impact of the strong pound on business, which he expected to steadily increase during 1997.

Dawkins said Argentina had shown the most noticeable signs of recent growth. "There are a lot of major projects underway in the country requiring airfreight support and we are also moving volumes of agricultural and computer equipment, along with hi-tech items," he noted.

These shipments are trucked from the UK to Luxembourg and Frankfurt, from where they are flown to Santiago and on to Buenos Aires by LAN-Chile, for which Air Logistics also acts as cargo GSA in Britain.
Observers note that the imminent arrival of the peak summer holiday season will see a big increase in passenger -- and therefore cargo bellyhold -- capacity from Britain to Florida.
Some of this space will be devoted to Latin America via transhipment services, but Florida, Atlanta, Houston and Charlotte will be also be markets fiercely competed for by airlines and their agents.
"We have achieved good yields and loads to and from Orlando during the winter with the Leisure International flights we use," said Viking's Durnin.

"But while loads are holding up, the onset of new summer compettion is already causing yields to stumble. It is always a tough market in the summer and this year it will be even tougher with a new player -- Laker -- involved," he added.
Last year, when a revived Laker started London Gatwick-Miami DC-10-30 services, it concentrated on all-economy passengers and did not bother with cargo. It has since changed this attitude.

From March 21, it has appointed Raeford to sell the 10-tonnes' capacity available on the carrier's daily Gatwick-Miami flights, twice-weekly Gatwick-Fort Lauderdale and (from June13) Prestwick-Orlando frequencies and weekly Gatwick-Orlando and Manchester-Orlando services.
"We are carrying a lot of flowers and vegetabes trucked in from Holland on these flights, plus interline cargo bound for Latin America and general traffic," said Raeford's Prince.
Virgin Atlantic Cargo is "well established in the UK-Miami market and still doing well", according to general manager commercial David Woodward.
Ex-Gatwick Boeing 747-200 flights on the route are currently operated five-times-weekly but will be increased to daily, with all departures from Heathrow, effective June 26.
Without giving details, Woodward said his Miami tonnage carried was up 13.2 percent so far this year compared to the same period in 1986, based on similar per tonne yields.
"The move to Heathrow will strengthen our position even further," he said.

UK cargo wholesaler International Cargo Marketing has noticed a weakening in its business to North America during the first quarter of 1997, said managing director Terry Greetham, who couldn't pinpoint the reason.
Virgin's Woodward gave these opinions on his airline's performance in different ex-UK U.S. markets:

Los Angeles: "A volatile market. In the past it was always a very strong route but capacity has recently been outpacing traffic growth. Our yields to LA are coming under attack compared to those on routes to the U.S. east coast."

New York: "A strong market which is fairly buoyant at present. This amazes me when all the capacity competition is considered. What has helped us is the trend of some carriers to downgrade Boeing 747s to twin-jets, which has reduced their cargo capacity."
Washington DC: "We only started on this route last summer and it has exceeded all our expectations. We have achieved almost double the traffic I initially forecast."
-Reuters Air Cargo Service Tel+ 44 171 542 7706; fax +5017
